claims.text: The stress–strain and thermoelastic behavior of HfNbTaTiZr is dominated by residual stresses.
The residual stresses arise from an intrinsic thermal-expansion mismatch between fine-scale α-phase or SIM-induced precipitates and a β-phase matrix.
Cold rolling and aging generate thermally induced internal stresses in HfNbTaTiZr.
These internal stresses alter dislocation mobility.
These internal stresses alter the apparent elastic modulus over a wide temperature range.
These internal stresses modify the high-temperature creep response.
Cold rolling followed by aging at 600–800 °C induces stress-induced martensitic transformation and fine α-phase precipitation in HfNbTaTiZr.
A solution or homogenization treatment can suppress precipitate formation and retain a more uniform, single-phase β structure.
The fine-scale α-phase or SIM-induced phases are embedded in the β-phase matrix.
The precipitate phase has a thermal-expansion coefficient different from that of the β matrix.
Cooling and thermal cycling generate residual stresses through the thermal-expansion difference between the precipitates and matrix.
The mismatch-generated stresses influence dislocation density and mobility.
The mismatch-generated stresses increase yield strength and alter strain hardening.
At high temperature, residual stresses impose additional energetic barriers to dislocation motion and thereby affect creep rate.
Relative to a homogenized single-phase control, the cold-rolled and aged material will have higher room-temperature yield strength.
Relative to the control, the cold-rolled and aged material will have higher room-temperature microhardness.
Relative to the control, the cold-rolled and aged material will exhibit a different elastic-modulus temperature dependence between approximately 293 and 1100 K.
Relative to the control, the cold-rolled and aged material will exhibit modified creep behavior at 1250 °C.
A homogeneous single-phase β structure minimizes internal residual stresses caused by phase-dependent thermal expansion.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis says residual stresses dominate the behavior and the predicted outcomes are attributed to them, whereas the uncertainty field concedes that their contribution may be smaller than classical work-hardening and precipitation-strengthening effects.

The conditions describe precipitate formation or thermal mismatch as the isolated variable, but the compared routes are cold rolling plus aging versus solution/homogenization. These routes also change work hardening, dislocation density, precipitation strengthening, recovery, grain structure, and thermal history, so differences cannot automatically be attributed only to residual stress.
